name: Saman v. Robbins
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California, District Judge Richard A. Paez)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, fatal shooting of an armed shopkeeper mistaken for a burglar, a single kick to a suspect during a chaotic officer-down scene held reasonable as a matter of law, jury verdict vacated, Monell claims
summary: A San Bernardino officer responding to a burglar alarm went to the wrong address, was shot in the chest by a shopkeeper carrying the day's cash, and killed the shopkeeper in the gun battle. A second officer arriving at the officer-down scene kicked a man who matched the suspect description once in the ribs after the man began to comply and then stood up. A jury awarded that man $34,000. The Ninth Circuit affirmed judgment for the first officer and vacated the verdict against the second, holding that the single kick in that tense, uncertain, and dangerous situation was objectively reasonable as a matter of law. It is taught as the personal body weapon case on the reasonable side of the line.
coverage: The full opinion and all footnotes were read from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/173/173.F3d.1150.96-55672.97-55789.97-55724.97-56684.97-56683.html. The archive file is headed 173 F.3d 1150 and lists the five consolidated docket numbers, which confirms the citation.
The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given.

Spelling. The court's caption is "Yousef SAMAN ... v. Daniel ROBBINS," and the short title is Saman v. Robbins. The decedent is spelled "Butres Samaan" and several family members are spelled "Samaan" while others are spelled "Saman." The court's footnote 1 states that the names were spelled inconsistently in the briefs, pleadings, docket, and record, that the court chose the spellings on its docket sheet, and apologized for any misspellings. Course materials that spell the case "Samman v. Robbins" do not match the court's spelling; the correct short form is Saman v. Robbins.
The two trials, the first jury's inability to reach a verdict, and the district court's rulings are described only as the Ninth Circuit described them. No subsequent history was verified.

Course materials describe the kick as following a command and a sudden movement during a volatile arrest, and the verdict against the officer as reversed. That matches the opinion. The brief notes that the court analyzed the kick on Officer Kimball's own account because the plaintiff's account of a beating did not involve Kimball.
facts:
On November 6, 1992, San Bernardino Police Officer Michael Blechinger received a radio dispatch that a burglar alarm had been activated at the rear of a store called Gibson's Healthful Living. The dispatcher gave the correct address, 570 South E Street. Blechinger had been to the store before and drove to where he thought it was, 391 South E Street. Gibson's had moved, and the space was now Mike's Ice Cream, owned by Yousef Saman. Just before Blechinger arrived, Yousef had counted the register cash for closing and had given his brother, Butres Samaan, a gun to protect them from robbers. The two went out the rear door to carry the cash to the building where they normally kept it.

Blechinger drove to the rear of the store and looked over a wall around a small parking area behind it. He saw a man holding a gun come out the rear door and another man standing in the doorway. Suspecting a burglary in progress, he ordered the man to drop the gun. The man, Butres Samaan, fired at Blechinger and struck him in the chest; a steel plate in his vest stopped the round. A gun battle followed and Butres Samaan was fatally wounded. Blechinger testified that he identified himself as a police officer four times, progressively louder, including once in Spanish, and there was evidence that he returned fire only after being shot and that Butres did not retreat until after firing several shots.

During the gun battle Blechinger broadcast that he had been shot, that the gun battle was continuing, and that he needed backup. He described the suspects, said there was more than one and at least one was armed, and said at least one had moved through the store toward the front. Officer Mitchal Kimball was among the first to arrive and came to the front of the store. He saw a man matching the description, later identified as Mohammed Alfaorr, and moved toward him with his gun drawn.

Two accounts of what followed were given at trial. Alfaorr testified that two officers held him off the ground after he was handcuffed while a third kicked him more than once in the chest, foot, and groin. The evidence showed Kimball was not part of that beating: Kimball was alone with Alfaorr until Officer Pritchett arrived, told Pritchett to handcuff Alfaorr, and left, and Alfaorr never identified Kimball as one of the officers involved. On Kimball's account, Alfaorr moved away as Kimball approached; Kimball ordered him to put his hands up and get on the ground; Alfaorr began to comply by lowering himself, then began to stand as Kimball got closer; fearing Alfaorr was armed, Kimball grabbed him, pushed him to the ground, and delivered a single kick to the rib cage to knock the wind out of him, then turned him over to Pritchett for handcuffing.

The survivors and estate sued Blechinger, Kimball, other officers, city officials, the city, and a deputy district attorney. Most claims were dismissed before or during the first trial; the first jury could not reach a verdict on the excessive force claims against Blechinger and Kimball. At the second trial the jury returned special verdicts for Blechinger, and the court entered judgment as a matter of law for him. The jury found against Kimball on Alfaorr's section 1983 excessive force claim and state battery claim, awarding $30,000 compensatory and $4,000 punitive damages. The district court denied Kimball's motion for judgment as a matter of law, dismissed the Monell claims on summary judgment, denied attorney fees to the dismissed defendants, and awarded reduced fees to Alfaorr. Multiple appeals followed.
holding:
Affirmed in part and reversed in part.

Officer Blechinger. The jury's special verdicts found that Blechinger identified himself as a police officer to Butres Samaan and that he had probable cause to believe Butres posed a threat of serious harm to him at the moment he fired the final shots. The plaintiffs' sufficiency of the evidence arguments were waived because they made no timely Rule 50(b) motion or motion for a new trial, and in any event the evidence was "clearly sufficient" to support the special verdicts. Considering the totality of the circumstances shown by the undisputed facts and the jury's findings, judgment as a matter of law for Blechinger was proper. The court found no error in the jury instructions, including the refusal of the plaintiffs' instruction on whether Blechinger created the danger, which the trial court found inappropriate on the facts and adequately covered by another instruction. Objections to the wording of the special verdict were waived.

Officer Kimball. Reviewing the denial of judgment as a matter of law de novo, the court found "no evidence on which a reasonable jury could find that Kimball used excessive force against Alfaorr," even construing the evidence in Alfaorr's favor. Alfaorr's account of a beating by three officers after handcuffing did not involve Kimball, who was alone with Alfaorr, directed another officer to handcuff him, and left. On Kimball's account, the court applied Graham: reasonableness is judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene rather than with hindsight, considering the severity of the crime, the immediate threat, and active resistance or flight, with allowance for split second judgments in tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving circumstances. Kimball was responding to a serious crime: an officer had been shot and was in a gun battle. He knew there was more than one suspect and at least one was armed. He saw a man who matched the description and had no way to know whether he was armed. The man began to comply with commands to get on the ground but then suddenly rose as Kimball approached. "Kimball's split-second judgment to administer a single kick to subdue Alfaorr in this tense, uncertain and dangerous situation in which one officer had already been shot was certainly objectively reasonable as a matter of law." The court cited Mendoza v. Block (police dog bites on a robbery suspect believed armed) and Forrester v. City of San Diego (pain compliance on demonstrators) as comparisons. The evidence was insufficient to support the verdict under section 1983, and the state battery claim failed with it because California battery by an officer requires unreasonable force. The court did not reach Kimball's qualified immunity argument. It vacated the verdict and directed entry of judgment for Kimball, which also reversed Alfaorr's fee award and mooted his cross appeal.

Monell claims. The claim that Roufai Samaan was illegally arrested under a city policy failed because his own testimony showed he voluntarily accompanied officers and the record showed no policy of illegal arrests. The excessive force policy claim was moot because, with no excessive force found against Butres Samaan or Alfaorr, there was no constitutional deprivation.

Attorney fees. The denial of fees to most prevailing defendants was affirmed, but the court reversed as to Officer Dana Bee, whose only involvement was drawing a scene diagram and whose claims the district court itself had found groundless.
notDecided:
Qualified immunity for Kimball. The court resolved the case on the merits and said it need not reach the alternative qualified immunity argument.

Whether the kick would have been reasonable on different facts. The court relied on the specific context: an officer shot, a gun battle, an armed suspect description, a match, and a sudden rise after beginning to comply.

Whether the beating Alfaorr described occurred or was lawful. The court held only that Kimball was not shown to be a participant. The opinion does not decide claims against any other officer for that conduct.

Whether Blechinger's address error or approach created the danger. The plaintiffs' proposed instruction on that theory was refused by the trial court, and the Ninth Circuit found no abuse of discretion; it did not analyze the theory on the merits.
inPractice:
Saman v. Robbins is the Ninth Circuit's clearest statement that a personal body weapon, used once, briefly, to gain control in a dangerous moment, can be reasonable as a matter of law. The facts that made it so should be named precisely: an officer down and a gun battle in progress, a broadcast that more than one suspect was involved and at least one was armed, a man who matched the description, no way to know whether he was armed, partial compliance, and then a sudden movement to stand as the officer closed. On those facts a single kick to the ribs to take the wind out of the man, followed immediately by handing him off for handcuffing, was within the range of reasonable conduct even though a jury had said otherwise.

Two cautions come with the case. First, the court analyzed Kimball's own account because the plaintiff's account of a beating did not implicate Kimball. Nothing in the opinion approves kicks to a handcuffed, controlled person; the plaintiff's version, had it been tied to Kimball, would have been a different case. Second, the lesson is one kick, one purpose, then control. The opinion describes a strike to end a sudden movement, not repeated strikes after resistance stopped.

Dr. Sowards teaches Saman as the reasonable side of the personal body weapons line: a strike after a command and a sudden movement during a volatile arrest, delivered briefly to gain control, with the verdict against the officer reversed. He pairs it with cases on the excessive side where strikes continued after control was achieved. The course spells the case Saman v. Robbins, as the court did.
trainIt:
Teach personal body weapons as a decision with a start and a stop. Use the Saman facts to build the start: a serious crime in progress, an armed suspect description, a match, an unknown weapon status, partial compliance, then a sudden rise. Have students articulate those facts before the strike. Then teach the stop: one strike to interrupt the movement, immediate transition to control and handcuffing, and a handoff or cover role once the person is controlled. Kimball kicked once and turned the man over to another officer; that sequence is what the court held reasonable.

Drill the contrast. Run the same scenario with the role player going prone and staying prone, or with the role player already handcuffed. Students must recognize that the justification for a strike disappears when the sudden movement does not happen or when control is already achieved. The plaintiff's account in Saman, officers holding a handcuffed man off the ground while another kicked him, is the picture of what the opinion does not approve.

Teach target selection and purpose. The strike in Saman was to the rib cage to knock the wind out of the suspect and incapacitate him for handcuffing. Students should connect the target to the purpose and avoid strikes whose purpose they cannot explain.

Teach the reporting lesson. Kimball's account survived because it was specific: what he heard on the radio, what he saw, what he ordered, how the man responded, and why he feared the man was armed. Have students write the Saman report from Kimball's position and critique whether each element of the Graham analysis is present.

Teach the posture: a jury verdict against the officer vacated on appeal as unsupported by sufficient evidence, with qualified immunity not reached.
caution: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive. Pin cites are not given because the archive text has no reporter page breaks. The kick analysis rests on Officer Kimball's own account, which the court used because the plaintiff's account of a beating did not implicate Kimball. The case should not be taught as approval of strikes on a controlled or handcuffed person.

applications.title: One strike to end a sudden movement
applications.body: The court held a single kick to the ribs objectively reasonable as a matter of law when a possibly armed suspect, at an officer-down scene, began to comply and then suddenly stood as the officer approached. The strike was followed at once by handcuffing by another officer.

applications.title: Name the context that justified it
applications.body: An officer shot, a gun battle in progress, a broadcast of multiple suspects with at least one armed, a match to the description, and no way to know whether the man was armed. Those facts drove the severity and immediate threat factors. Without them the analysis changes.

applications.title: The plaintiff's version was not approved
applications.body: Alfaorr described being held off the ground while handcuffed and kicked repeatedly. The court held only that Kimball was not shown to be part of that. Strikes on a handcuffed, controlled person are not what this case blesses.

applications.title: Spell it as the court did
applications.body: The caption is Saman v. Robbins. The decedent's name is spelled Samaan in the opinion, and the court acknowledged the record spelled the names inconsistently. Samman is not the court's spelling.

applications.title: Juries can be reversed in both directions
applications.body: A jury awarded $34,000 against Kimball. The Ninth Circuit vacated the verdict because no reasonable jury could find the single kick excessive on this record. The same de novo review can sustain a verdict against an officer when the facts support it.

quiz.q: Why did the Ninth Circuit vacate the jury's verdict against Officer Kimball in Saman v. Robbins?
options: Because a single kick to subdue a suspect who matched an armed suspect description and suddenly stood up at an officer-down scene was objectively reasonable as a matter of law, so the evidence was insufficient to support the verdict
Because the plaintiff was a convicted felon
Because the city had a policy authorizing kicks
quiz.teach: The court applied Graham's allowance for split second judgments in tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving circumstances and did not reach qualified immunity. The battery claim failed for the same reason.

quiz.q: What did the court say about the beating Alfaorr described?
options: It held the beating was reasonable
It held the beating was excessive and awarded damages
It held the evidence showed Kimball was not a participant, because he was alone with Alfaorr, directed another officer to handcuff him, and left
It did not mention the beating
quiz.teach: The court analyzed Kimball's own account because the plaintiff's account did not implicate Kimball. The opinion does not approve strikes on a handcuffed, controlled person.

quiz.q: What did the jury's special verdicts find about Officer Blechinger?
options: That he went to the wrong address and was therefore liable
That he identified himself as a police officer and had probable cause to believe Butres Samaan posed a threat of serious harm when he fired the final shots
quiz.teach: On those findings and the undisputed facts, including that Blechinger was shot in the chest before returning fire, the court affirmed judgment as a matter of law for him. The plaintiffs' challenges to the evidence were also waived for lack of a Rule 50(b) motion.
